uncited: This method computes the 2D screen-space basis vectors and eigenvalues for a 3D Gaussian splat by projecting its 3D covariance matrix through the view and projection matrices.

It transforms the 3D uncertainty representation into a 2D ellipse defined by orthogonal basis vectors and their scales, which are subsequently used to construct screen-aligned quads for rasterization.
It builds on [Projection Jacobian Computation](4272-projection-jacobian-computation.md), which provides the linearization of the projection function.
For a Gaussian with index `gid`, the first row is `covariance[gid*2]` and the second row is `covariance[gid*2+1]`.
Each element stores `basisVector1.x`, `basisVector1.y`, `basisVector2.x`, `basisVector2.y`.
*   `id`: Array of `u32` (used for permutation during sorting, though the calculation itself only produces the distance key).
The 3D covariance matrix $\mathbf{\Sigma}_{3D}$ is symmetric.
*   $\sigma_{xx} = \text{covariance}[gid \cdot 2].x$
*   $\sigma_{xy} = \text{covariance}[gid \cdot 2].y$
*   $\sigma_{xz} = \text{covariance}[gid \cdot 2].z$
*   $\sigma_{yy} = \text{covariance}[gid \cdot 2 + 1].x$
*   $\sigma_{yz} = \text{covariance}[gid \cdot 2 + 1].y$
*   $\sigma_{zz} = \text{covariance}[gid \cdot 2 + 1].z$
Assemble $\mathbf{\Sigma}_{3D}$ from the input arrays as defined above.

This variant describes how the computed basis vectors are used in the vertex shader to render the Gaussian.
It constructs a screen-aligned quad for each splat.
The centroid is transformed to NDC space.
The local quad coordinates (`inPos`, typically `[-1, -1]` to `[1, 1]`) are scaled by the basis vectors.
A `basisViewport` scaling factor (inverse of half-width/half-height) is applied to convert from pixel units (used in the Jacobian) to NDC units.
The final clip position is `ndcCenter.xy + ndcOffset`.
This ensures the Gaussian is rendered as a textured quad oriented according to the projected covariance.
*   **Time Complexity:** $O(1)$ per splat for the projection calculation.
The dominant cost in the pipeline is typically the subsequent sorting step ($O(N \log N)$ or $O(N)$ with radix sort).
*   **Memory Complexity:** $O(N)$ for storing the basis vectors and distances.
*   **Strengths:** Efficiently linearizes the perspective projection of Gaussians, allowing for correct 2D ellipse approximation.
The use of integer distances enables fast GPU-based radix sorting.
